mappings.note: Midpoint formula with algebraic expressions in both endpoints; two midpoint equations solve for x and y. Ratio 1:1 throughout, so LO-3.
Isosceles shown by two equal SIDE LENGTHS from the distance formula. No area, no midpoint.
Parallelogram established because the diagonals AC and BD share a MIDPOINT. This is the quadrilateral-property half of LO-3, not a side-length argument.
Rhombus but not square is settled by four equal sides plus one diagonal, all distances. Chosen over LO-3 because the diagonals' midpoints are never used.
Third vertex of an equilateral triangle from equal side lengths, with the origin condition picking the sign. Distance formula throughout.

Substituting a point into a line equation and finding where the line meets the x-axis. No distance, section, midpoint or area is used, and this frame has no outcome for lines or intercepts, so the goal code is the only one that does not distort.
The midpoint formula fixes p, and the resulting point is then tested against a line. The midpoint step is what the item actually assesses.
Median through A: D is the MIDPOINT of BC (LO-3) and AD is a DISTANCE (LO-1). Both steps are substantial, so both are cited.
Midpoints of two sides through A are given, B and C are recovered from them, and the midpoint of BC follows. Midpoint formula used three times over; nothing else enters.
Axis intercepts P and Q recovered from their given midpoint. Midpoint outcome.
The intersection of the diagonals is their common MIDPOINT, which yields the two missing vertices of the parallelogram. LO-3's quadrilateral clause exactly.
Two outcomes: the right angle is proved from squared distances (LO-1) and the AREA is then found from the vertices (C-4.2-LO-1). One of the few genuine area items in the chapter.
The RATIO in which the x-axis divides a segment, from the ordinate of the dividing point being zero. LO-2.
Ratio unknown, found as k:1 from the abscissa; the answer 1:1 is the outcome of the calculation rather than an assumption, so this is still section work and not the midpoint outcome.
Ratio 3:4 given, section formula solved backwards for the far endpoint B.
Ratio in which the x-axis divides the segment AND the coordinates of that point - both halves are section-formula work.
Same section computation as the paired item, with x squared plus y squared as the reported answer. Section formula solved for an endpoint.
AP = three sevenths of AB is converted to the ratio 3:4 and then the section formula locates P. Ratio conversion plus section, so LO-2.
Equidistance squared and expanded to prove y = 2x. Distance formula in algebraic form.
The midpoint theorem verified coordinate-wise: E and F come from the MIDPOINT formula (LO-3), then EF and BC are compared as DISTANCES (LO-1). Both are needed.
Two properties of a rectangle: diagonals BISECT each other (common midpoint, LO-3) and are EQUAL (distances, LO-1). LO-3 leads because the bisection is what LO-3 names.
Midpoints of all three sides, nothing more. The plainest midpoint item in the chapter.
Ratio unknown, found as k:1 from the abscissa, then the missing ordinate p. LO-2.
Points of TRISECTION - the section formula at 1:2 and 2:1. A 1:1 midpoint would not produce them, so LO-2 and not LO-3.
The midpoint formula plus the side condition a - 2b = 18 recovers k (LO-3), and the length AB is then a distance (LO-1). Two distinct steps.
